bibliographic.title: How Different AI Chatbots Behave? Benchmarking Large Language Models in Behavioral Economics Games
bibliographic.authors: Yutong Xie; Yiyao Liu; Zhuang Ma; Lin Shi; Xiyuan Wang; Walter Yuan; Matthew O. Jackson; Qiaozhu Mei
bibliographic.citation_apa: Xie, Y., Liu, Y., Ma, Z., Shi, L., Wang, X., Yuan, W., Jackson, M. O., & Mei, Q. (2024). How different AI chatbots behave? Benchmarking large language models in behavioral economics games. Preprint.

methodology.method_family: comparative behavioral benchmarking using behavioral economics games
methodology.study_design: cross-model benchmark of five LLM-based chatbot families across multiple behavioral economics games
methodology.sample_description: Five families of LLM-based AI chatbots; flagship models per family; checkpoints obtained as of July 31, 2024; models include OpenAI ChatGPT, Meta Llama, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and Mistral
methodology.technology_context: LLM-based AI chatbots evaluated in behavioral economics games including Dictator, Ultimatum, Trust, Public Goods, Bomb, and Prisoner's Dilemma

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The study empirically benchmarks behavioral patterns of LLM-based chatbots in behavioral economics games and does not address conversational governance, accountability, compliance, human oversight, auditability, or deployment in regulated environments.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the paper clearly concerns LLM-based chatbots and mentions deployment implications, reliability, trust, fairness, and risk in a behavioral-economics sense, the provided text contains no evidence on governance mechanisms, guardrails, observability, supervision, contestation, compliance, or regulated-domain application. The work is behavioral benchmarking rather than governance research.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: The mismatch with review scope is clear from title, abstract, introduction, and methods excerpt; no governance or regulated-context content is present in the supplied text.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal is based only on page 1-2 excerpts. Within its own aim, objectives and method framing appear clear, but results, limitations, ethics, and full analytic detail are not available in the provided text. Transferability to conversational governance in regulated settings is very limited.

cerqual.explanation: For the review's governance-in-regulated-settings focus, relevance is very low because the study measures chatbot behavior in economics games rather than governance practices or regulated deployment. Confidence in using this as review evidence is low despite a seemingly coherent empirical benchmark design within its own scope.

coding.subtheme: Comparative behavioral economics game performance across leading LLM families

synthesis.main_claim: Five leading LLM-based chatbot families exhibit common and distinct behavioral patterns when benchmarked across behavioral economics games, with implications for understanding their strategic preferences and deployment in decision-making roles.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a comparative behavioral profile of multiple prominent LLM chatbot families beyond prior ChatGPT-focused work, extending analysis across games testing trust, fairness, risk aversion, altruism, and cooperation.
synthesis.use_in_review: Not suitable as central or supporting evidence for conversational governance in regulated environments; at most peripheral contextual background on chatbot behavioral variability, with no direct governance, compliance, or oversight findings.
